summary:
Amazonas stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America on legal gender recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

That legal position coexists with lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten in Bello, Antioquia, in broad daylight, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon, and no one had been arrested as of reporting on 14 April 2025. Her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia, with President Petro ordering an urgent investigation and solidarity events held in several cities. Hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Caquetá, the department that borders Amazonas to the north, armed groups gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers against trans women; trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". The Attorney General's Office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases. Colombia recorded 41 trans women killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, and the Attorney General's Office logged 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country; same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's pattern is a wide gap between formal protection and street-level outcomes: the same country that moved gender-marker changes to a notary in 2015 recorded 41 trans women killed in 2023 and 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission framed this directly as institutional progress set against daily lived experience.

Organised violence is a distinct layer above opportunistic crime. Kill-list and "social cleansing" flyer campaigns in Guajira since March 2024 and in Caquetá name trans people explicitly, and reporting on the Millerey case describes calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict rather than isolated attacks.

The non-recognition of transfemicide by the prosecutor's office, as reported in the Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024, means the killing of a trans woman can be recorded and prosecuted as an ordinary homicide, which affects how such violence is counted and how families are treated. This is a national-level institutional finding rather than one specific to Amazonas.

Amazonas itself is a low-population Amazonian department with a small urban centre, where the national pattern may be mediated by distance, the presence of armed groups operating across the north of the region, and reliance on officials and health services concentrated in Leticia. The sources give no department-level reporting either way.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports any incident, law, enforcement action, facility or official practice specific to Amazonas. The department-level picture is unresolved: whether the national protections are applied in Leticia and the surrounding municipalities, and whether local officials or armed groups behave as described for Antioquia, Caquetá or Guajira, is not sourced here.

The claim that the Attorney General's Office does not recognise transfemicide, and records such killings as ordinary cases, rests on a single Guardian investigation published 30 July 2024 and is presented at national level; no confirmation from a second source or any statement on how Amazonas prosecutors classify these deaths is available.

Victim counts differ across sources and periods: 41 trans women killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 by the Attorney General's Office. These are national totals with different date ranges and categories, not directly comparable, and none are broken down by department.

Reporting on Sara Millerey's death gives two accounts of the sequence and timing of her death (drowning in a creek on 5 April 2025 in early coverage; a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon in the 14 April 2025 account). Whether anyone was subsequently arrested is not resolved in this inventory.
